transcript: The men tell him there's so much gold here that all the people in California working together couldn't take it out in 50 years. Instantly, dollar signs flash in Brandon's eyes. But instead of brainlessly jumping into the river to find gold himself, he crafts what is perhaps the greatest marketing stunt in American history. Brandon returns to San Francisco and quickly begins purchasing every single pickaxe, shovel, and gold pan he can find in the area. He ships them all to his store in Sacramento and tells his employees to price these items at extreme markups. He then puts the gold dust he received as payment into a glass bottle and steps out onto the streets of San Francisco. He holds up the bottle and loudly shouts gold! Gold on the American River! And the townspeople near him all stop their daily routines and turn to look. He holds out the bottle, and as it sparkles in the sun, he continues to shout his message over and over again gold on the American River! Brandon's plan works, and the news spreads through the town like wildfire. In a very short amount of time, nearly 75% of the men in San Francisco raced east to try to strike it rich. On their way to Coloma, they all stop at the only store with tools along the way, Brandon's general store in Sacramento. In the first nine weeks of the Gold Rush, Brandon makes $36,000, an equivalent of $1.4 million today, and He quickly becomes the richest man in California. But while Brandon's marketing stunt worked out better than he could have ever imagined, it LED to some unintended consequences. News of gold in California spread throughout the world, and by 1850, San Francisco had exploded from a small port town of less than 1,000 people to a city of over 25,000. The massive boom of fortune seekers brought unprecedented levels of crime and lawlessness, and the local government, with its small police force, just couldn't keep up. Gangs of thieves and murderers begin to roam the streets of San Francisco freely without any fear. The worst of these criminals are the Sydney Ducks, a ruthless gang of ex cons from Australia. They set fires to buildings to distract the police while they loot businesses, and anyone caught in their way often ended up dead. On the rare occasions the police managed to catch them, they just bribe corrupt officials and walk out of jail Scott free. On May 4th, 1851, a fire set by the Sydney docks burned down around 2,000 buildings, which was more than half the entire city and caused over $10 million in damages. Brandon watched that fire rip through the city, and he decides that enough is enough. On June 9th, 1851, he brings together a group of well known citizens and businessmen. He tells them that the police are worthless and that if they want the crime to stop in their town, they would need to take justice into their own Hands! Everyone in attendance agrees. And so, on that night, they form a committee of vigilance to take back their city from these criminals. Conveniently, this committee did not have to wait long to take action.

You decide not to think too much. Thinking too much will only open something you cannot close. Days become weeks. Weeks become a pattern. You learn the pattern and you keep your face smooth. The older women say a smooth face is your greatest tool. They say this without pity, which is almost its own kind of pity. Then one morning, you cannot eat the bread. Your stomach turns at the smell of the oil. The mistress of the household watches your face over her clipboard of accounts. She sends for a physician. He is a priest doctor who smells of natron and old incense. He presses your wrist, checks your eyes, asks you questions in that flat, professional voice. He tells the mistress something in a low tone. The mistress nods. You are pregnant. The house shifts around you like a current changing direction. Your food portions double. A servant is assigned to walk with you in the garden. Mornings and evenings the lady of the house visits your chamber, which she has never done before. She stands in the doorway and looks at your stomach with an expression that is not quite hatred and not quite grief, but lives somewhere in between them. Then she leaves without speaking. That look will live. In you longer than the visit. You ask your mother in your mind, to put her hands on you. She doesn't answer because she is 100 miles south and doesn't know where you are.

transcript: That night, I couldn't sleep. I kept checking the hallway through the peephole in my apartment. It got worse. One Saturday, I saw him on the platform in my train station. He didn't say anything, just stood there at the other end, watching me. I rode three extra stops and walked home on a different day. The next day, I had told my manager, David. He was concerned, but unsure of what to do. He's not a guest here anymore, he said. We could ask him to leave if he shows up again. But unless he threatens you. He paused. I felt helpless, so I started documenting everything. Dates, times, what he said, where I saw them. I kept the gifts as evidence. The final stroll came on a Wednesday afternoon. I was working the desk, and William walked in like he owned the place. Jessica, we need to talk, he said. I stood up. No, we don't. You need to leave. He stepped closer. I care about you. I think you feel the same. My hands were shaking. I picked up the phone and dialed in YPD. I then told him, you need to leave now. He stared at me, stunned. Then he laughed. You're overreacting. No, I said loud and clear. I'm not. Two officers arrived within 10 minutes. William, of course, tried to play it cool, acting like it was all a misunderstanding. But I showed them the log, the notes, the gifts. One officer asked if I wanted to file a report. Yes, I said. They escorted him out. It wasn't dramatic, but it was final. William hasn't come back since. Some nights, I still feel nervous walking home. I still glance over my shoulder. But each day, I feel a little stronger. Working at the front desk, I've Learned how to smile when I don't want to. How to be polite when someone doesn't deserve it. And how to say no when someone crosses the line. Most of all, I've Learned that keeping quiet doesn't keep you safe. Next time, I'll speak up sooner. It's been about a year since I called the police on William. Sometimes it feels like a lifetime ago. Other times, it feels just like last week. I still remember his face. The way he looked at me. Like I was something he owned. That look still shows up in my dreams. But life is better now. A lot better. After everything that happened, I decided I needed a change. I quit my job at the hotel. Three months after the incident. I couldn't sit behind that front desk anymore. Every time the doors opened, I felt a jolt of fear. I'd scan the lobby for him for weeks. I kept expecting him to come back. He never did. But the fear stayed with me. Quiet, heavy. Sitting in my chest like a stone. I moved apartments, too. Nothing fancy. Just a small studio in Queens. I like it there. It's Quieter. And my neighbors are friendly. There's a little grocery store around the corner and a park where I walk in the evenings. It's really peaceful, in a way Manhattan never was. I started seeing a therapist after I moved. At first, I didn't really want to go. I didn't think I needed it. But talking to someone really helped. I realized I was still carrying so much fear, anger, and shame. She told me that none of it was my fault. And I think finally I believe her. I now work at a bookstore. It's a small place, locally owned, with warm lights and shelves that go up to the ceiling. The owner, Dana, is kind and funny, and she treats me like a person, not just an employee. I get to help people find stories they'll love. I get to talk about books, drink tea behind the counter, and feel safe. And I never have to wear a name tag again. Sometimes I think about who I was back then. The girl behind the front desk, trying to stay polite, trying to not cause trouble. I really wish I could go back and tell her that it's really okay to speak up, it's okay to protect yourself. That being nice to someone doesn't mean you owe them anything. I still check over my shoulder when I walk home. I keep my phone in my hand. I double lock my door every night. That part of me might never Go away. I've accepted that. But I'm not scared all the time now. I'm stronger. I'm more careful. Yes, but I'm also more sure of myself. I know what I will and won't allow. I know how to set boundaries. And I know that if anyone ever tries to cross them again, I'll be ready. William took something from me. A sense of ease, maybe a bit of trust in the world. But he didn't take me. I'm still here. I'm still living. And finally, I feel like I'm in control of my own life again.
